enrichment.short_title: Du Pont and S.T. Dupont trade mark opposition appeals on clothing marks
key_facts: E.I. Du Pont sought to register DU PONT in class 25 (clothing); S.T. Dupont opposed and also sought to register a stylised S.T. DUPONT mark in the same class.
Neuberger J allowed STD's late surnominal objection under sections 9 and 10 of the 1938 Act and upheld section 11 and section 5(4)(a) objections; EIDP appealed with leave.

STD relied on Paris telephone directory evidence that Dupont was a common surname; EIDP had long used DU PONT on fabric swing tickets but not as a trade mark indicating a connection with finished clothing.
STD's menswear use through Harvey Nichols mini-shops was limited; EIDP contended STD's mark would pass off against EIDP's fabric reputation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with leave from Neuberger J's decisions on two linked trade mark opposition appeals from the Registrar.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Neuberger J's orders set aside and the Registrar's decisions restored, so EIDP's DU PONT application may proceed and STD's application is refused.
enrichment.ratio: Registry telephone-directory guidelines cannot substitute for the section 10 test of whether a mark is capable of distinguishing in the United Kingdom; a late surnominal amendment prejudicing the applicant should not be allowed without proper opportunity to adduce evidence; section 11 requires actual likelihood of deception or confusion among a substantial number of persons, not merely prior use of a similar non-distinctive surname; use of S.T. DUPONT on clothing was liable to be prevented by passing off against EIDP's goodwill in DU PONT for fabrics; appeals under section 18 of the 1938 Act are subject to CPR Part 52 and are generally by way of review, not a full rehearing.
legal_issues: Whether Neuberger J was wrong to allow STD's late amendment raising a surnominal objection and to admit fresh telephone directory evidence
Whether DU PONT was registrable in Part B under section 10 despite being a common French surname
Whether STD's limited use supported a section 11 objection
Whether STD's mark should be refused under section 5(4)(a) of the 1994 Act for passing off
Whether trade mark appeals under section 18 of the 1938 Act are rehearings or reviews and how CPR rule 52.11 applies

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on fraudulent entry burden of proof.

enrichment.short_title: Burden of proof in fraudulent entry illegal entrant case (Ullah)
key_facts: Mr Ullah entered the UK in March 1994 on a foreign spouse visa following a marriage in Pakistan to Zahida Bashir, a British citizen and his cousin.

The Home Office treated him as an illegal entrant from September 1995, relying on Miss Bashir's letters to the Home Office and her later interview assertion that she had telephoned him in Pakistan telling him not to come.
Maurice Kay J dismissed judicial review, holding Article 6 did not apply and that the Secretary of State had discharged the Khawaja standard of proof.
The appellant denied the alleged February 1994 telephone call; the judge had no oral evidence from Miss Bashir and relied mainly on documentary material.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against Maurice Kay J's dismissal of judicial review of the Chief Immigration Officer's illegal entrant decision.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the Secretary of State had not proved fraudulent entry to the requisite high degree of probability.
enrichment.ratio: In illegal entrant cases the Secretary of State must prove entry by fraud to a high degree of probability (Khawaja); where the decisive allegation rests on an untested hearsay assertion by the former spouse about a single telephone call, and the documentary evidence is internally inconsistent, the burden is not discharged even though Article 6 does not apply to immigration removal proceedings and the absence of cross-examination of Miss Bashir was not procedurally unfair.
legal_issues: Whether Article 6 ECHR applied to immigration judicial review proceedings
Whether the appellant was entitled to a witness statement from or cross-examination of Zahida Bashir
Whether the Secretary of State satisfied the Khawaja burden and standard of proof on fraudulent entry

enrichment.short_title: Summary judgment on debt repayment agreement barred by limitation
key_facts: Mr Gadhok, former company secretary of Gomba Holdings, claimed Mr Shamji owed about £150,000 plus interest arising from a property transfer to satisfy Gomba-related liabilities.
The claim form was issued in November 2001, but the parties disputed whether repayment was due almost immediately, when Gomba or Shamji had money, or at some later point.

Patten J allowed Shamji's appeal from the recorder and held the arrangement was not a loan contract excepted by section 5(2)(b), that repayment terms were sufficiently certain, and that on Gadhok's own evidence the debt became repayable in 1989 and was statute-barred.
Gadhok's successive pleadings and witness statements gave materially inconsistent versions of the repayment terms.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with limited permission against Patten J's order allowing Shamji's appeal and dismissing the claim on summary judgment/limitation grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Patten J's order affirmed and the claim remains struck out as hopeless.
enrichment.ratio: On a CPR Part 24 application the court may look beyond pleadings to witness statements and contemporaneous documents; where a claimant's evidence on when funds became available is contradicted by his own inconsistent accounts and does not establish that Shamji or Gomba could pay the debt owed to him (as opposed to his wife), summary judgment on limitation is appropriate; an agreement to repay when a debtor or related company has money may be void for uncertainty, in which case the debt becomes immediately repayable.
legal_issues: Whether the arrangement was a contract of loan for section 5(2)(b) purposes
Whether repayment terms were sufficiently certain to be enforceable
When the cause of action accrued and whether limitation had expired
Whether Patten J was entitled to decide on summary judgment that Gomba had funds to repay in 1989
What evidence may be relied on at the interlocutory stage under CPR 24

notes: Complete Commercial Court trial judgment on cargo contamination and demurrage.

enrichment.short_title: Ship-to-ship oil transfer water contamination and demurrage claim
key_facts: Fal Oil sold about 75,000 tonnes of high-viscosity fuel oil to Petronas Trading (Petco) via ship-to-ship transfer from MV CENTAUR to MV DEVON off Port Sudan in February 2001.
Shore tank certificates at Yanbu showed 0.2% water within the 1% contractual limit; after discharge in Singapore/Malaysia the cargo showed substantial seawater contamination.
Experts agreed roughly 1,500 metric tonnes of seawater had been substituted for oil somewhere before Caltex sampling, but the mechanism and location remained unexplained.
Saybolt surveyor Mr Pantouvakis inspected both vessels at the STS; Petco bore the burden of proving excessive water at the point cargo passed DEVON's manifold.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Commercial Court on breach of quality warranty and demurrage claims following ship-to-ship transfer and delayed discharge.
enrichment.outcome: Petco failed to prove on the balance of probabilities that the cargo exceeded permitted water at transfer; Fal Oil's claim succeeded on quality. Demurrage clause construed as an indemnity tied to charterparty demurrage, not an independent buyer obligation.
enrichment.ratio: Where about 1,500 tonnes of seawater replaced oil before discharge but both pre- and post-STS contamination on CENTAUR and post-STS contamination on DEVON remain plausible and neither can be excluded, the defendant seller does not meet the burden of proving contractual off-specification water at the critical point (Popi M principle); in a C&F contract, a demurrage clause referencing charterparty rates is in nature an indemnity for demurrage actually incurred by the seller as shipper, not a free-standing buyer liability where no charter demurrage is due.
legal_issues: Whether Petco proved excessive water content at the point cargo passed DEVON's manifold
Where the substitution of seawater for oil most likely occurred
Whether Fal Oil's surveyor evidence and STS measurements were reliable
Whether the contractual demurrage provision created independent liability or an indemnity

notes: Complete Court of Appeal judgment on implied surrender of assured tenancy.

enrichment.short_title: Implied surrender of assured tenancy on transfer to new housing association flat
key_facts: Ealing Family Housing Association let Flat 2, Kingswood Road to Mrs Sharon McKenzie under an assured weekly tenancy from April 1997; her husband Mr McKenzie occupied as spouse with section 30 Family Law Act 1996 rights.
After marital breakdown Mrs McKenzie left Flat 2 in February 2000 and accepted a new tenancy at 38 Invicta Grove from 17 July 2000, signing a notice to quit Flat 2 on the same day.
Mr McKenzie remained in Flat 2; Ealing treated him as an illegal occupier and sought possession against him.
The county court judge found an implied surrender by operation of law on 11, 17 July or 22 January 2001 despite invalid short notices to quit.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against Brentford County Court possession order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; implied surrender on 17 July 2000 upheld and possession order against Mr McKenzie stands.
enrichment.ratio: Surrender by operation of law depends on unequivocal conduct by landlord and tenant inconsistent with continuation of the tenancy, not merely intention; where a tenant accepts a replacement tenancy on the landlord's policy of one tenancy only, signs a notice manifesting immediate termination, moves into the new property, and the landlord closes the old rent account and treats the remaining occupier as trespassing, there is an implied surrender even though vacant possession could not be delivered because the spouse remained in occupation.
legal_issues: Whether Mrs McKenzie effected a valid surrender by operation of law
Whether surrender requires actual vacant possession to the landlord
Whether invalid short notices to quit preclude finding surrender
Whether later requests for a further notice undermine an earlier implied surrender

enrichment.short_title: Boundary fixed by physical features where transfer plan too small scale
key_facts: Dispute between Sidbrook Farm (claimant Gillon) and Lower Knapp Farm (defendants Baxter) in Sidbury, Devon, over about one-fifth of an acre.
The 1985 transfer described land only as edged red on a photocopied 1:3,650 plan with thick pen edging equivalent to a two-lane road width on the ground.
Scaling the plan produced a yellow uncertainty band; the only vehicular access to Barn Field OS 5888 was via a timber gate and green track lying west of that band, alongside fence line E-F.
The trial judge visited the site and held the boundary ran along fence E-F; defendants later sold and settled with Gillon except on costs.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission against Exeter County Court declaration on paper-title boundary.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; boundary declaration along line E-F on the final analysis plan affirmed.
enrichment.ratio: Where a transfer plan is on a very small scale and for identification only, exact boundaries must be determined by construing the instrument in light of surrounding physical circumstances; it is unrealistic to draw a boundary east of the only gateway and track giving access to a transferred field, and the judge was entitled to fix the line on an longstanding fence where the plan cannot delineate precise boundaries.
legal_issues: Whether the 1985 transfer plan definitively fixed the boundary
How to construe parcels clauses referring to plans edged in red
Whether physical topographical features override scaled plan ambiguity
Effect of declaration that all boundaries are transferors' property to maintain

notes: Complete judicial review judgment upholding section 94 certification for Jamaica.

enrichment.short_title: Section 94 clearly unfounded certification upheld for Jamaican asylum claim
key_facts: Jamaican claimant entered on a six-month visitor visa in February 2002 and claimed asylum in April 2003 after arrest as an overstayer.

He claimed imputed PNP political affiliation as an informer after witnessing JLP violence, prior assaults by JLP members, and persecution as a perceived homosexual because he worked with a gay employer.
The Secretary of State refused asylum and human rights claims and certified them clearly unfounded under section 94(2), removing in-country appeal rights.
Jamaica was on the designated states list; country evidence showed high gang-related violence especially in garrison communities but ongoing law enforcement initiatives.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal of asylum/human rights claims and section 94(2) clearly unfounded certificate.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; certification and refusal upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A section 94 certificate is lawful where, after assessing the claim against known country background, no legitimate view could allow success: sufficiency of protection does not require elimination of all risk but a practical operating legal system (Horvath); the claimant's informer fears were not comparable to Brown (witness to gang murder needing witness protection); perceived homosexuality claims failed for lack of substratum of past violence or substantial discrimination; internal relocation within Jamaica away from St Andrew (South) garrison area was reasonable and not unduly harsh.
legal_issues: Whether Jamaica's inclusion on the section 94 designated states list was lawful
Whether there was sufficiency of state protection against gang/political violence and homophobic attacks
Whether internal relocation within Jamaica was viable
Whether past ill-treatment prevented certification as clearly unfounded
Meaning of clearly unfounded under section 94

enrichment.short_title: Macedonia asylum claim certified clearly unfounded over family honour threats
key_facts: Ethnic Albanian Roman Catholic claimant from Macedonia arrived in July 2003 with his Roma Muslim partner Lindita Islami.
Primary fear was death threats from her family opposing marriage between a Muslim and a Catholic; secondary claims related to village discrimination against their mixed ethnicity/religion.
Secretary of State certified asylum and human rights claims clearly unfounded on 10 July 2003; Macedonia was a designated state under section 94.
Threats were localised to the village and family; claimant did not assert the family could find him elsewhere in Macedonia.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of section 94(2) clearly unfounded certification of asylum and human rights claims.
enrichment.ratio: Where persecution feared from a partner's family is geographically limited, internal relocation elsewhere in Macedonia is a viable answer and the claim is bound to fail; village-level discrimination falling short of Article 3 severity cannot support refugee or human rights protection; Article 8 does not apply where feared ill-treatment would occur only in the receiving state (Razgar territoriality principle); on designated-state cases the claim must be clearly unfounded and arguable claims cannot be certified.
legal_issues: Whether the claim was clearly unfounded for section 94(2) purposes
Whether internal relocation within Macedonia was unduly harsh
Whether Article 3 was engaged by discrimination short of persecution
Whether Article 8 applied to feared treatment on return
Whether there was insufficiency of protection against non-state actors

enrichment.short_title: SHAC harassment injunctions — companies cannot be victims under the 1997 Act
key_facts: Five linked actions by Japanese-linked UK pharmaceutical and industrial companies and named employee representatives sought injunctions against SHAC, ALF, ARM and activists campaigning to close Huntingdon Life Sciences.
Campaign included threats, hoax bombs, firebombings, abusive letters, home protests and damage targeting company directors and employees.
Gibbs J had already granted HLS injunctions under the 1997 Act; these claims sought similar relief against suppliers/customers of HLS.

Owen J held 'person' in section 1 does not include a corporate body, following DPP v Dziurzynski, but representative employee claims could proceed and interim injunctions with exclusion zones were appropriate.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory hearing in the Queen's Bench Division for injunctive relief under section 3 of the Protection from Harassment Act 1997, following without-notice and interim orders.
enrichment.outcome: Corporate harassment claims failed on construction grounds; injunctive relief to proceed for individual claimants and employees under CPR 19.6 representative proceedings, subject to final order drafting on exclusion zones.
enrichment.ratio: On proper construction of the Protection from Harassment Act 1997, 'person' in section 1 means an individual human being and not a limited company, so companies cannot be victims of harassment under the Act; individual employees may bring representative claims under CPR 19.6 where they share the same interest in freedom from harassment; exclusion zone injunctions may restrain lawful highway use where necessary to protect against unlawful harassment, balanced against Articles 10 and 11.
legal_issues: Whether a company can be a victim of harassment under section 1 of the 1997 Act
Whether representative proceedings under CPR 19.6 were appropriate
How unincorporated associations should be joined as defendants
Whether interim exclusion zone injunctions were justified and proportionate
Whether SHAC reportage of unlawful acts amounted to encouragement of harassment

enrichment.short_title: Income support urgent payment — asylum claim must be made on arrival

statutes_considered.title: Geneva Convention Relating to the Status of Refugees

key_facts: Claimant arrived at Gatwick from Yemen at 10.30pm on 29 August 1999 but did not claim asylum until 31 August 1999.
Regulation 70(3A) defined an asylum seeker for urgent case payments as someone who submits a claim for asylum on arrival in the UK.
She said an agent controlling her entry told her not to claim at the airport and took her by taxi to her sister's address.
Income Support Appeal Tribunal and Commissioner held she was not entitled to urgent payment; regulations have since been superseded.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal with permission from a Social Security Commissioner against dismissal of appeal from an Income Support Appeal Tribunal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; literal interpretation of 'on his arrival' upheld and urgent payment refused.
enrichment.ratio: Regulation 70(3A) requires an asylum claim to be submitted on arrival in the United Kingdom; that language cannot be stretched to 'first effective opportunity' where the claimant voluntarily placed herself under an agent's control without physical duress, and a person using an agent is responsible for the agent's conduct unless clear physical compulsion is shown.

Whether use of an entry agent excuses delayed asylum claim
